messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 55-year-old bomb disposal technician who was deployed to a coastal village in West Africa after a catastrophic earthquake triggered a tsunami. He spent thirty-six hours pulling bodies from the wreckage and debris, working in chest-deep water that kept rising without warning. What stayed with him most was the sound—the roar of the water followed by the screams, then the silence, then another wave. He had been trained to stay calm in controlled explosions, but this was chaos without a timer, without a plan, without any way to predict what would come next. In the months that followed, he found he could only recall fragments: the smell of wet concrete, a child’s shoe floating past, the way his hands shook as he tried to lift a collapsed wall. The rest felt missing, like a film reel with whole sections cut out. He would start to remember, and then something in him would slam the door shut before the full picture could arrive. And when the fragments did surface, what rose in him was not sadness but a white-hot rage—at the ocean, at the government that had sent him, at himself for not saving more people.

Back home in Chicago, Kofi returned to work but found the world had become a landscape of hidden dangers. Loud noises—a truck backfiring, a door slamming—sent his body into a full defensive posture before his mind could even register what had happened. His heart would pound, his muscles would lock, and for a split second he was back in the water. He started reacting as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, and the unpredictability of daily life—traffic jams, sudden schedule changes, a colleague raising his voice in a meeting—felt unbearable. The more his body reacted before he could think, the more he came to expect danger everywhere, scanning every room for exits, every conversation for the first sign of conflict. Shouting was the worst; it triggered a cascade of physical alarm that left him breathless and furious, and the memory of the tsunami would surge back, incomplete but overwhelming, and the rage would return.

To manage this, Kofi began avoiding anything that could be stressful. He stopped attending team briefings, stopped meeting friends, stopped driving on unfamiliar roads. He kept his mind occupied all the time—podcasts, audiobooks, constant music in his earbuds—so there was no silence for the memories to break through. But the constant mental distraction exhausted him, and when he was too tired to maintain it, he would overeat in the evenings, numbing himself with food until he could fall asleep. This avoidance, however, only made the world feel smaller and more dangerous. The less he confronted unpredictable situations, the more threatening they seemed when they did arise. A sudden noise on a quiet street would make him flinch, and the flinch itself would trigger a flashback—a full sensory return to the wave—and then the rage again, and then the shame of having lost control. He began to see threats everywhere, and every threat triggered a memory, and every memory made him more vigilant, and every moment of vigilance wore him down further.

His wife, Amina, noticed he had stopped laughing. He no longer wanted to go to their daughter’s soccer games because the crowd noise felt unpredictable. He had started eating dinner alone in the basement, listening to a history podcast at full volume so he wouldn’t have to hear the television from upstairs. He was certain that if he let his guard down for even a moment, the memories would flood back and he would drown in them. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at the grocery store: a child dropped a glass jar, and Kofi hit the floor, covering his head, his heart slamming against his ribs. A security guard had to help him up. He could not stop shaking. He knew then that the world he was living in—a world of constant alarm, of fragmented rage, of hiding from his own mind—was no longer sustainable. He was afraid of what he might do the next time a sound surprised him, and he was desperate to find a way back to the person he had been before the water rose.
